props.title: Delivering Milo

sections.content: **Delivering Milo** (2001) represents a unique entry in the metaphysical comedy genre, following in the footsteps of **Heaven Can Wait** (1978) and **It's a Wonderful Life** (1946). Starring Anton Yelchin and Albert Finney, the film explores pre-birth existence through the story of Milo, an unborn soul reluctant to enter the world. While it didn't achieve widespread recognition, it shares DNA with more celebrated existential comedies like **Defending Your Life** (1991) and **The Family Man** (2000) in its examination of life's value through supernatural intervention.

sections.content: The early 2000s saw several films wrestling with metaphysical themes through a lighter lens. **What Dreams May Come** (1998) and **Bicentennial Man** (1999) approached existence and humanity with similar philosophical undertones. **Delivering Milo** stands out for tackling pre-existence rather than the afterlife, joining rare company with films like **The Pre-Natal Classroom** (1977) and segments of **The Soul Keeper** (2003). SUBHEAD: Coming-of-Age and Existential Themes

The film's unique perspective on birth and beginning aligns it with unconventional coming-of-age narratives. While movies like **Big** (1988) and **13 Going on 30** (2004) explore youth through magical age transformation, **Delivering Milo** examines the very threshold of existence. Albert Finney's performance as Elmore echoes his work in **Big Fish** (2003), another film dealing with life's extraordinary possibilities through a magical realist lens.
